clusters.title: Expected sold-out 409s counted as k6 HTTP failures
clusters.description: k6's built-in http_req_failed classifies the buy path's expected 409 responses (sold_out, idempotency_conflict) as failed requests unless the generated script overrides response classification. The docs explicitly call clean sold-out runs a valid demonstration.

members.note: Worst variant: no override at all, and the raw rate feeds terminal grading, so the flagship surge presets always finalize failed.
Script has custom expected-outcome counters and checks, but http_req_failed is still copied raw into the persisted summary — cosmetic/history damage, not terminal-status damage.

notObserved.note: GLM's generated script overrides the k6 response callback; its self-review lists clean sold-out handling as verified and its k6 roundtrip test asserts failure_rate == 0 for all-sold-out traffic.

clusters.title: Run-scoped ERP behavior / backpressure frozen into the run snapshot but not applied
clusters.description: All three implementations freeze per-run ERP chaos and backpressure config into the run snapshot and validate/display it; applying it at runtime is where they diverge.

members.note: Nothing applied: Mock ERP uses only the global chaos store, worker concurrency fixed from env.
Same shape: resolveControl ignores runId, worker reads every knob from env; global chaos leaks between runs structurally.
Narrower variant: request-scoped ERP config IS applied, except the TPS window, which remains a single global counter.

clusters.title: The real k6 execution path is effectively untested
clusters.description: The load-generation contract (real k6 compatibility, output parsing, completion reporting) lacks reliable automated coverage in all three implementations, via different mechanisms.

members.note: Real-k6 integration test self-skips silently when k6 is absent; parsers otherwise validated against canned JSON.
Same silent skip, aggravated: the test sits in the infrastructure-free unit lane and k6 is absent in the environment, so it never runs. Graded HIGH by GLM.
Different mechanism: no skip involved — the production SpawnK6Runner path is simply never instantiated by any test.

clusters.title: Synchronous observability work on the accepted-buy hot path
clusters.description: All three await best-effort dashboard/telemetry work inline on the winning reservation path, adding latency to the one-second surge target for no correctness benefit.

members.note: One awaited Redis PUBLISH before the durable write.
Several awaited publishes plus redundant Redis reads (inventory state re-read, queue.getJobCounts).
Heaviest variant: multiple PostgreSQL aggregate count queries awaited per accepted reservation.

clusters.title: Watch dashboard can present stale or previous-run state as current
clusters.description: Different mechanisms, same user-facing failure: the live watch surface shows data that does not belong to the current run or the current moment. Related to the documented recovery-baseline / events-as-hints contract.

members.note: Recovery keeps the live overlay with no run-change detection; a sold-out-only run shows the previous run's outcome counts throughout.
Recovery is never re-fetched on reconnect or terminal events, so recovery-sourced counts freeze for the session.
Live events are applied with no runId/timestamp guard, so a delayed previous-run event overwrites fresher state.

clusters.title: Run-sale eligibility on the buy path does not fail closed in every case
clusters.description: Each implementation has a gap where the run-scoped eligibility guard can be bypassed or go stale, letting buys decrement stock they should not — the severity of the gap varies widely.

members.note: Largest gap: no run-scoped eligibility signal exists at all; wrong-run buys leak permanently unreconcilable holds and closed runs stay buyable.
Gate exists but is skipped for null-runId catalog buys against run-owned offers, leaking a Redis hold per rejected write.
Gate exists but closure is best-effort: a failed Redis close leaves a closed run accepting.

clusters.title: ERP confirmation is not idempotent across worker persistence failures
clusters.description: The worker calls the ERP before durably recording the confirmed transition, and the mock ERP does not dedupe by orderId, so a transient persistence failure after a successful ERP call double-confirms downstream.

members.note: Graded Low: bounded to duplicate downstream confirmations; order state stays correct.
Graded High, and a unit test explicitly locks in the double confirm; persistent local failures can even end with the order failed after downstream acceptance.

notObserved.note: Not raised in GLM's self-review. Its slice 3 lists persist-before-side-effect ordering as verified, but ERP-confirmation idempotency across a confirm-then-persist failure was not explicitly addressed.

clusters.title: Pending-persistence protocol edge cases
clusters.description: Loose grouping: distinct defects in the Redis-hold pending-persistence protocol (what happens when the durable write fails after Redis secured stock). Same protocol, different failure modes.

members.note: Pending holds are never durably reconciled — pending forever, stock held with no order.
Race: a concurrent idempotent replay reads the pending sentinel before the loser writes it and promises an order that will never exist. Opus's reconciler otherwise exists.

clusters.title: A single transient failure can leave a run permanently non-terminal
clusters.description: One missed message or one crash at the wrong instant leaves the run stuck in a non-terminal state, blocking all future starts until manual admin intervention.

members.note: Crash between summary write and lifecycle transition strands the run in draining; the already_finalized early-return prevents any retry.
Fire-and-forget completion report: one failed POST leaves the run active with no retry or reconciliation path.

notObserved.note: Opus's appendix records guarded duplicate/concurrent finalization and startup reconciliation as checked and sound; no equivalent stuck-run path was reported.

clusters.title: Documented dev/runtime commands drift from the implementation
clusters.description: Commands or operational recipes that the docs present as working but that fail or behave differently when actually run.

members.note: Root test:db:migrate still points at a not-implemented placeholder that exits 1, while documented in three places.
Five documented per-package test commands fail with ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_RUN_NO_SCRIPT (verified at runtime).
Wipe-and-rebuild recipe omits runtime:up; health-check docs list readiness check names that no longer exist.

clusters.title: Readiness reports healthy while a critical dependency is down
clusters.description: Readiness endpoints that gate healthchecks and smoke tests pass while a dependency the service cannot function without is unreachable. (GLM's related finding F22 is vocabulary drift on the readiness surface rather than a false-green probe, so it is not a member.)

members.note: API readiness checks only Redis config presence; a down Redis reads as degraded/200 while every buy 503s.
Worker readiness trusts BullMQ isRunning(), which stays true while the consumer is disconnected and consuming nothing.
Load-orchestrator readiness validates only that the API URL string is non-empty, never that the API is reachable.

clusters.title: Notification recording vs finalization contract
clusters.description: Mirror-image handling of the same design question — must notifications settle before a run finalizes? GLM finalizes without waiting (undercount); GPT waits unconditionally (a lost enqueue fails the run). Worth deciding the intended contract when comparing implementations.

members.note: Settled gate excludes notifications, so notificationsRecorded is best-effort at finalization time.
Finalization blocks on notificationsRecorded == confirmedOrders with no repair path, so one lost enqueue drives business_drain_timeout.
